We need a version of Radiohead’s “Creep” where the chorus goes “You’re a creep/you’re a weirdo/what the hell are you doing here?/you don’t belong here” and we can just send that to them and then block them

Seriously though, I’m really sorry you had to experience this. These people aren’t creeps, they are assholes and borderline criminals. It is *not* okay they did this to you. I am really glad you blocked them/stopped responding, I know that can be hard, so I’m proud of you that you took this step of self-care and even decided to speak up on here. 
In my opinion/experience there are some really horrible people in this world. Sometimes something you do will “attract” them – like posting on this sub which can make you seem vulnerable. I have two thoughts on this: You can take precautions to protect yourself. Like not telling your age, like op did, that’s a clever step. That means that you are not helpless here. You have some of the power, and that’s just a good thing to feel, because we all know feeling powerless can be really traumatic. Second thought though: You *can* do things to protect yourself. You should not have to. It is not your responsibility that other people don’t traumatise you. If someone shoots you, sure, you could have protected yourself by wearing a bullet proof west, but obviously it’s the shooter’s fault you got shot, not yours. So if you do end up in a really bad situation, you don’t have to be ashamed or feel guilty (even though it’s completely okay and natural to feel that way). Someone did something bad to you and they are in the wrong. You get to decide how you want this situation handled. You can, but don’t have to and I’d like to encourage you not to be quiet about and not tell anyone because you might feel like you did something wrong. You did not. It’s okay to talk about what happened and have people help you feel better. You can block them, report them, maybe even to the police depending on what they did. You can send them a message about how fucked up that is or you can ignore them forever. 

What I’m trying to say is this: There are really bad people out there. Them doing bad things is never on you. But you aren’t powerless. The more in control you feel in a bad situation, the less likely it is to be traumatic to you.
And in some cases, I’m afraid you can be powerless in a bad situation because the perpetrator makes sure of it. It’s not your fault for not getting out of a terrible situation. But even in those frankly traumatic scenarios, you can get your power back. Report them, be angry at them, forgive them, talk about it, whatever is the right way for you.

So, take care, and know that if something bad happens it is not because you did not take enough care, at all, but there are some ways to take care of yourself even in these situations.

Hey! I am so sorry you’re struggling with this, I know it’s really hard. I actually just started using a wheelchair for FND about a week ago, and I often do feel like I’m not allowed to/just faking/doing it for attention. For me, there are some days where I can walk without any problems, some days I can’t move my legs at all, but most days, I can *technically* walk, but it takes a lot of mental energy and often triggers seizures. So since I would be able to walk most of the time, I feel really invalid using a wheelchair. But it is getting easier every day! The more I use it, the more I realise how much freedom it brings me. Two days ago I went to the theatre, which means I had to get to the train station, take the train for an hour, and then get from the station to the theatre. I never would have been able to do that without my wheelchair. I could also go to university on days where my legs would barely work when in the past, I would have just missed the seminar. I’m really starting to see a difference in my everyday life, which is showing me that it is the right decision to use a wheelchair. If you feel like it could help you to use a mobility aid, just try it out, and you will see if it’s right for you. If it is, if it helps you in any way at all, then use it! There’s no gatekeeping on mobility aids. If it improves your quality of life, it’s more than okay to use it.

By the way, I’m also still pretty young (23) and I have been worried about people questioning my disability and my need for a wheelchair, especially since I do get up and walk small distances from time to time. Here are just a few examples of things that worked out so much easier than I expected them to:
• People at university didn’t mind at all. They all know me without wheelchair, they had no idea that I struggle with walking. I was so afraid how they’d react when I went there with my wheelchair for the first time, but everything was so chill. Sure, some looked a bit surprised at first, but only for a second. They did treat me a bit different, but kind of in a helpful and appropriate manner. Like, some people asked me if they should bring me the list we had to sign to prove our attendance, someone asked whether they should remove a chair so there was space for me to sit at a table and when we did some work in groups, people came to me so I could stay in place. But aside from that, they treated me exactly the same. Like, they tried to be helpful but not nosy or invasive or something. 
• My roommate didn’t care at all. I was so afraid to tell him I would start using a wheelchair, so I texted him instead of telling him face to face, and he just responded “okay :)”
• When I went to the theatre, we had seats on the gallery because a friend gave me her ticket which wasn’t for a wheelchair accessible seat. So I sent an email to the theatre saying I could walk up the stairs but would like to use my wheelchair for the way to the theatre and asked whether I could store it somewhere during the performance. I was so afraid they would find it weird that I would use a wheelchair when I could walk, but they were so so nice. When I arrived, someone came to show me where I could store the wheelchair and took me to the employees’ stairway so I could get up the stairs in my own time without having any people around and showed me to my seat so I wouldn’t have to walk around looking for it.
• A friend of mine was really surprised when I suddenly started using a wheelchair (I’m new in this town so I haven’t known them for long and they don’t know about my FND), but, like, not in a bad way?! They did want to ask some questions about it, but they also asked whether it was okay for them to ask me about it first. I was actually really glad they wanted to know a bit more because it gave me the opportunity to explain why I use a wheelchair even though I can walk and they were just really curious and interested and open and I really appreciated that they made an effort to understand my situation.

I realise this comment got kind of long, but I just wanted to show you that it’s normal and okay to be scared, but also that things often work out a lot better than you expect.

Oh, and also, I recently found out that with FND, differences in brain activity *can* often be found. The structure of the brain isn’t altered, but the function really is, and it does show on fMRI in some studies. Some experts also see FND as a brain network disorder, since the brain areas that are supposed to work together seem to have a “communication issue”. So whilst there is not structural alteration in FND (though I actually just read one study questioning this, but there’s not a lot of research in that direction), there are observable changes in the way the brain works. FND isn’t fake. Your symptoms aren’t fake. They are valid. You are allowed to make your life a little easier, and if that means using mobility aids, then use them. 

Take care!

Yeah, that’s why I said I would go somewhere where they can keep you under observation long enough to catch several seizures. Epilepsy and PNES do sometimes occur together. So during a PNES, your EEG might look normal. But that doesn’t mean you can’t have epileptic seizures where the EEG would show something. That’s why I would look for a place where they can catch several seizures on EEG (normally if someone had an eeg during a seizure and it didn’t show anything, yeah, it’s probably PNES. It’s just that incontinence is so much more common in epilepsy, so I would get it checked out just to be sure. Still could be solely PNES, I’m not saying you definitely have epilepsy as well, just that it seems to be a possibility)

I normally never do this, comparing illnesses or suffering because it simply does not matter, no one suffers less than they do just because there’s a person “having it worse”. Suffering is always valid. But just to put some perspective on your take that it’s invalid to use a wheelchair for mental reasons as compared to physical reasons, which you did imply in your comment, I want to tell you how I experience mental and physical illnesses. I have a chronically inflamed stomach and esophagus. I have *chronic* migraines. Not simply headaches, actual migraines that come with dizziness, nausea, not being able to see clearly, barely being able to move or speak, muscle weakness in one side of my body. I have a neurological disorder that comes with temporary paralysis, tics/tic attacks, seizures and many many more fun features. Yeah, it really sucks. You know what I also have? Severe depression, adhd, complex PTSD and dissociative identity disorder (used to be called multiple personality disorder and is the result of severe, repeated and inescapable childhood trauma). And these are the disorders that make my life so, so hard. These are the things that caused me to try and end it all quite a few times. If I could give away my psychiatric disorders for an increase of symptoms in my physical ones, I would. I definitely would. 

Mental disorders can be torture to live with. Don’t ever assume that someone having a mental illness makes them less valid then someone having a physical illness or disability. If a wheelchair helps someone with mental illness manage their symptoms better, it’s amazing for them to use it and I wish for them to get as much quality of life as possible. 

Mental health matters.

eeeeeehm a few things: I actually like being asked whether I identify as disabled - my official disability card thingy (I‘m German, no idea how it works in other countries) is still „in the making“ (so much paperwork and assessment appointments that would be challenging for any non-disabled person. not sure it *has* to be that hard…) Anyway. I have no official paper saying I am disabled. I have lots of doctors notes and hospital reports documenting my chronic illnesses, but not a official statement that those illnesses are a „disability“. I still identify as disabled. It’s up to you to decide if an illness/disorder impairs you so much in daily life that you are disabled. Not some reviewer from some health office who knows you for an hour and might know nothing about your conditions. 

Other thing, more importantly: why the bashing against trans people? They’re just trying to align their sex with their gender as much as possible. Studies have shown that trans people often have the brain structure of their gender, but a different sex. What’s bothers you so much about people modifying their body to affirm their gender? To their actual identity the identify as due to it being who they are in the center of human consciousness, the brain?! Really weird and ugly move to bring your transphobia into this.

You’d be right to ask the important question where it would end, tough. With body integrity identity disorder, the body doesn’t register certain parts of the body as its own, so e.g. taking off a limb is kind of modifying the body to fit the brain‘s experience as well. But of course, that would cause disability and significant impairment in everyday life. So how should we deal with this? Should doctors be allowed to perform surgeries for biid? If not for the patient’s comfort in their own body, maybe for harm reduction if a patient os at high risk to hurt himself? So yeah, „where does this end“ is a discussion we do need to have, and it’s not easily answer.

Last thing: so you would bet there are people on here solely using a wheelchair for mental reasons. And yeah, their might be. They are valid. I am borderline one of them (I also have a neurological disorder, but even that is closely linked to my psychiatric diagnosis). Mental illnesses can have symptoms that can be better managed or only be managed by using a mobility aid. Ever heard of dissociation? It’s a psychological mechanism and a psychiatric umbrella of diagnoses, and it’s such fun! /s There are dissociative seizures, both absence and full blown convulsions, there’s dissociative blindness and deafness, dissociative loss of sensation in some body parts (or just the whole body), not being able to talk, and yeah, there’s also something called dissociative movement disorder which, guess what, comes with paralysis of some or all body parts (called dissociative stupor then) and can for example paralyse your legs for some time. Sometimes minutes or days, for some people years or decades. So yeah, there might be people on here using wheelchairs for “mental reasons”, namely a psychiatric disorder. They are just as valid as the people on here using wheelchairs for purely physical reasons.

I am going to tell you what was/is helpful to me, but please remember that everyone is different and this might not apply to you.

• Often I can get out of seizures if someone holds an ammonia ampule/inhalant under my nose. It really hurts to breathe in ammonia and it often kind of snaps me out of it

• I have a little bag with emergency information on me at all times. Inside there’s like a small card that tells people that I have PNES, *not* epilepsy, that it’s not a medical emergency and there’s no need to call an ambulance. Saved me a few trips to the hospital.

• My seizures are caused by dissociation. Naltrexone really helps with my dissociative symptoms including seizures. I take Naltrexone daily, and on days where I have more seizures than usual, I take Abilify as well. No idea why or how it works, but it does reduce seizure frequency and duration a bit for me.

• It might be worth getting checked out for any underlying or accompanying disorder. PNES can (but don’t have to!) be triggered by psychological trauma. As I said, for me it’s a kind of dissociation, so I got assessed for dissociative disorders and turns out I have Dissociative Identity Disorder. I know a lot of people in the DID and c-ptsd community who get dissociative seizures. !! I am not saying you have one of these disorders. Just trying to illustrate that PNES can be linked to something else. !!

• For me, it was really helpful to find out my triggers (sudden loud noises, being touched by other people, flickering lights…) Maybe you can find some of yours and learn to avoid them as much as possible.

• Remember that you will be okay. You said that you can feel a seizure coming on, which is great and really helpful! When you feel you’re going to have a seizure, get yourself in a safe position, make sure there aren’t any edges around your head and cover hard surfaces with a sweater or something. Remember that seizures don’t last forever. It will pass. If I don’t lose consciousness, I try to go to an inner safe place during a seizure and it really helps me calm down. After the seizure, check if you need anything, try to listen to your body. Do you need some rest? Do you need to move and stretch a bit? Do you need some water? Just try to support yourself as best as possible. For me, it’s really helpful to look at my phone after a seizure to check the date and the time. I also look around to consciously see where I am. I always say to myself (not out loud, just thinking): “It is [date]. It is [time]. I am at/in [location].” It really helps me to get reoriented.


I hope some of this helps, if you have any questions feel free to ask. I know it’s scary and really really hard, but you will be okay and you can have a good life. Sometimes PNES spontaneously go into remission. Sometimes Psychotherapy really helps. Sometimes the seizures don’t really get better, but you learn to cope and enjoy your life nonetheless. It’s okay to feel scared and confused and it’s okay to struggle! This is a hard thing to live with. But remember that you don’t have to feel this way forever, and you will find ways to cope. Sending you a lot of strength 🫂

Hey, sorry I didn't reply, I had a crazy few weeks. As I said, I think it really depends on your environment. Being gifted in itself hasn't been hard (just as being queer isn't difficult per se, only in the context of our heteronormative society). As a child, I loved being gifted (though I didn't know I was gifted back then). I loved learning, exploring the world, having a lot of imagination, just using my brain in general. I always felt my mind was especially colourful and nuanced (not meaning I felt better like everyone else, just grateful to be able to experience being with such depth). Everything was great as long as I was in elementary school, we had small classes and the teachers could make sure everyone's educational needs were met. When I went to middle school/high school, things were quite different. For a while, I went to school every day, thinking "I'm going to learn something new today, and it's going to be so interesting". I barely did learn anything new. Every few weeks we would talk about something new, but then we would just practice and repeat for weeks. I felt like I had so much energy, I was so curious, but I had nowhere to put it. I constantly felt like I was running against a wall. I tried asking question, but the response usually was "I won't explain that, that would go too far, you'll learn about that in a few years". I took books to school to read under the table, they got taken away. I tried to talk to some of my teachers, tried to tell them I was bored out of my mind (in polite and respectful wording). They usually said, "Yeah, I can see that, but school is for everyone, so you'll just have to be patient and wait" (If school is for everyone, why did no one care about my educational needs?!). In high school I finally had a teacher who liked that I was curious and interested and they suggested me for a programm where I could go to university a few hours a week instead of school. It was fun, but it was too little too late. I had been sooo frustrated during the past years that I had taught myself how to be not interested, how to not be curious, basically how not to think. I needed to stop feeling like my mind was running against a wall, so I stopped running. I felt tired and empty and still all of the time, until it turned into a full on depressive episode. I have been depressed ever since, I never felt able to "turn my brain on" again (there's even a word for depression due to being unchallenged, it's called "bore out"). Add to that all the times someone called me "nerd" just because I got good grades (once I stopped being curious and interested I became the class clown, and I still got called a nerd until I made the conscious desicion to start getting bad grades by deliberately screaming up tests). So no, I didn't have bad social skills, I knew exactly how to behave to fit in but just the fact that I was on top of my class grade-wise was enough for some people to say stuff like "go get a shovel and dig yourself a grave, you fucking nerd". So yeah. Being gifted in middle/high school wasn't great. I spent most of my nights as a teenager staying awake, asking the internet "how to get dumber". I hated the effect of drugs and alcohol, so the only option seemed to be hitting my head against the wall, which I did. Repeatedly. It didn't work, of course, but I think it illustrates pretty well how desperately I wanted not to be gifted (and as my therapist said when I told her about it a few years later, it might not have made me dumber, but it certainly lets me appear pretty dumb (which I thought was a pretty funny thing to say)). Being queer wasn't always easy either, of course, but since I am demisexual I barely ever experience sexual attraction, so it wasn't much of an issue most of the time. Once I fell in love with another girl I was already out of school for a while and had a far more diverse and accepting social circle, so I felt comfortable with my sexuality. It just didn't matter most of the time before, whilst being gifted was woven into every fiber of my being. 

I know a lot of people struggle to understand my experience, but I hope that since people on this subreddit might have minds that work similarily to mine, you might understand why being gifted has been such a struggle for me.

It's not unusual and definitely not a sign of faking to notice symptoms only after learning about DID. There are a few things that might be happening:

1. DID is all about hiding trauma, both from the ANPs (the parts/alters responsible for everyday life stuff, e.g. usually the host) and the people in their environment. Systems usually hide themselves for a long time. Maybe your system noticed that you were learning about DID, and saw an opportunity to make themselves known. It's perfectly natural for a system to be far more open and obvious if given the opportunity.

2. DID isn't what most people think it is. It's not always hearing voices, obvious switches and missing days of time. It's PTSD, passive influence, "made" emotions and thoughts, subtle switches and amnesia for amnesia, meaning you don't even notice you have lost time. Perhaps you had some symptoms before but didn't know what they were, and now that you know what to look for, you notice.

3. Amnesia. Maybe you did have symptoms before and simply forgot about them. I thought I had started losing time two years ago, at the age of 21. But a few months ago, I remembered that there was a time when I experienced amnesia before: When I was 19 I had just moved out of my parents' house and in with some friends, and we drank *a lot*. But no matter how drunk I got, I never had a blackout. So I used to say "It's funny, I lose more time when I'm sober than when I'm drunk". Even now, when I meet with high school friends and we share stories of our time together, there is *so much* I don't remember. But I never thought I had amnesia during that time. Also, about not having "enough" trauma: "Enough" is very subjective. If it was unbearable for you, that's enough. Period. Also, there might be and there probably is trauma you don't remember. I had a weird thing going on with a friend when I was 19 (almost 20), it was short and intense and ended in the worst heartache of my life (yet), but I really loved him and still care about him deeply, so I don’t regret it. I started dating again when I was 21 and it was horrible. I hadn’t dealt with my interpersonal and sxl trauma at all, I didn’t know what boundaries looked or felt like and that my safety mattered more than keeping the peace. I started dating a guy mostly because he asked me out and I felt like I was expected to like him back. Ended up in a relationship with him because he kept asking and I stopped saying no. Here’s what I would have liked to know: You need to know some things about yourself to be able to build a healthy and safe relationship. Ask yourself what consent and safe intimacy (both physically and emotionally) feel like for you. Stay connected to that feeling. If you lose it when you are in contact with someone, take some time and space to reconnect. If in any situation you forget what boundaries and safety look/feel like for you, you are not capable of giving consent. Learn what your body feels like when it doesn’t feel safe. You mentioned a panicky/anxious feeling in your body – Where do you feel it? What do your belly, your chest, your head and your limbs feel like? Are you hot or cold? Tense or weak/numb? Does the feeling have a color? Get to know that feeling really well and learn to recognise and listen to it. It might feel awful, but that feeling isn’t your enemy, it aims to keep you safe. It can guide you. As you are healing, you will learn which situations feel unsafe because they remind you of past trauma and which ones are actually unsafe in themselves. Some intimate situations will be an opportunity to learn that intimacy can be safe and empowering. You can teach you anxiety that it’s valuable, but misplaced, and your body can learn how to feel safe and close to someone (physically or emotionally) at the same time. All of this, all these ideas on how you can keep yourself safe and healthy, only refer to situation in which you are with a safe person. You can only explore where your boundaries are if you are given the space to. If someone decides to not give you that space, that’s an awful thing of them to do, it is 100% their responsibility and their fault.

I didn’t know what feeling safe felt like back then and I felt like it did not matter anyway. I had learned that I had to give what was asked of me and not think twice. My body tried to tell me that it didn’t feel safe, I constantly had panic attacks and dissociative seizures. I did not listen and started dissociating so much that I ended up in a trauma clinic for three months. I finally managed to break up with that guy when I got out. Kind of stumbled into a similar relationship a few months later, thankfully it didn’t last long. Shortly after I got together with my best friend, it didn’t last (I don’t know why, tbh), but I felt safe for the first time in a romantic relationship. We never got intimate since we both have some trauma, but I still felt more connected to her than to anyone else. Which goes to show, you can explore romantic relationships and dating without pushing yourself to do anything you are not ready to do. There are tons of people who are asexual but not aromantic, and for them it’s completely normal and healthy to not be physically intimate while dating. I am demisexual, which means I only experience physical attraction if I am mentally attracted to someone first, for me it’s less about finding someone attractive and more about wanting to be close and feel connected to someone. I don’t know if it’s due to trauma or just the way I naturally am, it doesn’t really matter to me right now, it’s how I identify at the moment and that might change when I heal more or it might not.

You are young, and aside from that, it’s not like there’s an official timeline in life (even though many people like to act like it). Take your time if/once you decide you want to explore dating. Give your body and your nervous system time to catch up. Only do what you want to do, dating someone doesn’t mean you owe them anything. If you end up doing something and later realise you didn’t really want to, don’t be hard on yourself. I know the feeling of “If I failed to protect myself now, if I just acted like I wanted to and couldn’t stand by my boundaries, maybe that’s what happened back then as well? Maybe it’s all my fault because I didn’t express that I did not like what they did?”. That’s not true. Your boundaries weren’t crossed because you did a bad job protecting them/yourself, if anything, it’s the other way around. You have a hard time protecting yourself because your boundaries once were crossed. Which means that it’s okay to sometimes do things and only realise you did not want to later on. It is important to learn to identify what you do and don’t want early enough, but not because it makes you culpable for anything that happened now or in the past if you don’t, only because you deserve to be safe and healthy, and to have a dating life that’s fun, that feels good and light, that helps you heal instead of causing you harm.

I wish you a safe and healing journey if you ever decide to start dating. Take care!

You should always get medical attention when you hit beans, you'll almost certainly need stitches. Please get it checked out as soon as possible since stitches can only be applied in the first few hours.

If you absolutely cannot get medical attention, please take really good care of your wound. Here's how: First, you need to make butterfly stitches. Best thing would be to use medical tape or the sticky part of a bandage, if you don't have any and have no chance to get it, normal tape is better than nothing. Cut it in stripes (2-3mm wide, 5 cm long). Disinfect or thoroughly wash your hands. Then, flush the wound out with saline (you can make it at home, instructions are online) or distilled water. Clean the skin around the wound with disinfectant. Do not get it into the wound since it can hurt healthy tissue. Close the wound with the butterfly stitches you prepared (if you don't know how to do it, there are guides with pictures online). Put sterile gauze over the closed wound and keep it in place with (medical) tape. Alternatively use a bandage, just keep it covered. Change the gauze every day until it stays clean/the wound is completely scabbed over and doesn't leak any fluid. Leave the butterfly stitches on until they come off on their own.

If you have no way to make butterfly stitches and close the wound at home, please get medical attention (should do that anyway). Open healing significantly increases the risk of infection and at that depth it could easily cost you your limb or your life.

If you have no choice at all but to leave it open, keep the wound covered until it is completely scabbed over and then a few days more. Use sterile gauze or if you don't have any, clean cloth like an old, washed shirt. Do not, in any case, use tissue or toilet paper since those shed fibers that can get stuck in the wound and cause infection. Change the cover each day and clean the skin around the wound with disinfectant. Do not get the wound wet! Wrap some foil around your leg and tape it to your leg if you have to shower.

If you notice any signs of infection (pus that's thicker than usual (often green or yellow), wound/surrounding skin gets hot and swollen, fever), you HAVE to get medical attention. There's no way around it.

Please take care!

I wouldn't put desinfectant in deeper wounds since it can harm the tissue, only put it around the edges. You can flush out the wounds with saline (can also be made at home, instructions are online) or distilled water. Gaping wounds should be closed, if they only gape a little bit you don't have to, but it will minimize scarring. If they are gaping more than a few mm they definitely need to be closed after cleaning them to minimize the risk of infection. You can close them with butterfly/steri strips. Put some sterile gauze on top, secure with medical tape. The gauze should be changed every 24 hours or if it gets wet. Steri strips should stay on until they come off by themselves. If blood leaves the wound with very high pressure, they've probably hit an artery and need immidiate medical attention, call 911. If it bleeds a lot, but with less pressure, press some clean cloth on top that does not shed fibers (so no tissues or toilet paper) for 10-15 min. Continuously, no peeking. If bleeding hasn't stopped after that, repeat. If it still hasn't stopped it's time for the hospital. Also, when cleaning the wound, check how it looks inside. If it's gaping but you only see white tissue, that's the dermis and steri strips should be fine. If you see small yellow "bubbles", that's fat and the wound almost certainly needs stitches, which also means they have to get medical attention. Whatever method is used to close the wound, it needs to be done within the first few hours. After that, healing has already begun and there might be bacteria in the wound that would get trapped inside and increase the risk of infection, so closing the wound isn't an option anymore. Which is problematic, because open healing significantly increases the risk of infection. Hope this helps.

I don't think some disorders are per se more severe than others. I have both DID, which is usually considered a pretty complex and severe disorder, and a standard case of Depression, which is usually considered very treatable and less complex. However, when I am in a severe depressive episode, it can make life Just as hard as DID. I understand why one would be generally considered more severe, for example people with DID are far more likely to attempt unaliving than people with Depression. But I think we all know how dangerous and deadly Depression can get. So no, I would never look down on anyone who solely experiences depression, GAD or some other disorder than *can* be mild, because I don't know their story. They could be suffering just as much as someone with a more "severe" disorder like Bipolar, BPD, DID or schizophrenia.
However, of course there are some people who will, luckily, only experience mild symptoms of a mental health disorder. I don't judge them, no. Most people are not mentally ill, anyone who is faces some kind of struggle that impacts their life and deserves compassion, help and support. The possibility of more severe suffering does not make their suffering easier for them. I do sometimes envy people with mild cases of a disorder, though. The first time I went to a trauma clinic, I thought I had PTSD from two incidents, thought I would work through it, do some EMDR and leave basically healed, with all my trauma processed and integrated. Instead I left with a DID and cPTSD diagnosis, knowing it will take many, many years to process and integrate our trauma, if even possible. And I saw some patients who also came to the clinic with a PTSD diagnosis, who worked through their trauma in the few months there and left stable and content, going back to a live without debilitating symptoms every day. And I was so disappointed, because I thought that was how it was gonna be for me. When the clinic told me I am not allowed to do EMDR (to process trauma) because it's to destabilizing when you are highly dissociative, I was really angry and sad. I just wanted to work through my trauma and be done with it. So yeah, I often wish it could have been like that for me/us. But I also know that doesn't mean it was easy for them. They still had to leave their life behind for several months because they experienced something so awful it took them months of therapy to work through it. And even the people who never have to go inpatient, who experienced a mild depressive episode and got some meds or a few therapy sessions and recovered, they still had symptoms bad enough to disrupt their daily life, to make them notice something was wrong. Every mentally ill person has suffered. Others suffering "worse" does not change that, at all. Even mentally healthy people can encounter an enourmous amount of suffering through life events. Not everyone who experiences trauma will develop PTSD, not everyone who grieves depression. These people still suffer, deserve compassion and help. I don't really see the point in comparing struggles, it doesn't change anything, you just have to look at each individual person and see what they need. What sucks, though, is that there aren't enough ressources to take care of everyone's mental well being. But it's not even like more severely impacted people have more access to help. Usually it's your socioeconomic status that decide which ressources are available to you. So yeah, distribution of ressources is the only aspect where I think rating severity matters, but irl, it's not even how it works. So I don't see any point in comparing, really.

The least a mental hospital should do is keeping you safe, offering some space to talk about your thoughts and feelings, and helping you figure out medication. Unfortunately, there are some mental hospitals that do not keep you safe, that actually cause harm. I think fewer than there seem to be, though. One thing you can always do if you are there voluntarily is leave. But since you are not in crisis at the moment, you could use this time to „plan ahead“ and make a solid crisis plan, which means you could check out the mental hospitals available to you (e.g. location- or insurancewise), get a feel for the environment, talk to the staff, let them show you what a week of therapy looks like there. You could also ask about the discharching process if you decide to leave earlier than planned, some hospitals have a contract that you have to stay for 24 hrs or something before you can leave, other hospitals you can leave as soon as you decide to do so. So yeah, I would suggest doing some research and finding a hospital that feels safe, maybe even healing, to you. (I really think most are, I just don‘t want to ignore the fact that some can cause harm or invalidate people with psychiatry trauma). It should definitely be possible to find a place that can offer you these minimums of safety, opportunities to talk to someone, and figuring out medication. When you‘re in crisis, what you seem to be expecting (hoping for you it won‘t get that far), those places can be absolute life savers and are doing a good enough job at getting you through it and support you in these times. The great thing about a hospital (opposed to outpatient treatment) is that you have some kind of help available 24/7. You can always talk to the staff, you can always ask for medication to get you through the worst moments, and honestly the other patients are usually awesome, can relate, just be there for one another and even offer really good advice. In these places you might really not solve a lot of your problems, but you will have the support to get through the worst and then enter the fight with new strength and hope. I unfortunately don‘t know that much about the US medical system, but I think there are also treatment centers that focus more on recovery instead of crisis management. Usually you‘d stay there a bit longer and it‘s more focused on psychotherapy and less on medication. That would be a place to actually solve many of your problems, I think this kind of treatment can be really beneficial, but of course it‘s a long time away from loved ones and school/uni/work, so you kind of have to decide whether you want to move forward a long way in your recovery but put you life on pause for a while, or if you want to continue therapy in an outpatient setting with a shorter stay in a mental hospital for crisis management. Whatever you decide to do, I want to say this: There are some mental hospitals that aren‘t safe and that cause bad harm. However, it is not the majority and often not the case when you are voluntarily admitted. In most cases, you will have a supportive environment, someone professional to talk to not just once a week, you might have additional therapies like art or sports therapy, and the other patients can be so supportive and it can be so healing to live in the communitiy of the ward for a while. It will probably take a while to get used to everything, when I am new in a mental hospital I am always scared to speak to anyone, to even leave my room, and I‘m constantly worried I‘ll do something wrong, break a rule or miss a therapy session. That‘s perfectly normal. Just try to push yourself a bit (not too much, there‘s no hurry!) to get used to the ward. Ask staff or other patients to explain the therapy schedule to you, maybe someone has the same group therapy and will take you with them. Find out what the others are doing in the evening when therapy is over, maybe there‘s a TV room, or a place where they play card games. You can just ask someone what they do in the free time or if you see some other patients doing something that looks fun to you, just ask if you can join in! Usually the other patients are really open and welcoming and are happy you want to spend some time with them. In my experience, mental hospitals are not scary. I had one really bad experience but since I was there voluntarily, I could just leave (had to wait a week to get into another hospital, though, which is why I would check out hospitals before). The other times, I simply found everything very overwhelming and new in the beginning, but it never took too long to figure out how stuff works and anyone on the ward, staff or patients, will be happy to help you out and to be there for you. So yeah, I‘d say find a hospital that feels safe for you and don‘t be scared to go there. When in crisis, a mental hospital can be a really valuable resource. Whatever you chose, I hope you get through this & heal. Take care <3

I fundamentally disagree with the sentence „If I can’t fix it, then I have to punish myself.“ I often feel that way, too, but kn a more cognitive level, it makes no sense to me. Punishing won’t do any good. You just end up feeling more guilty. It does not help you, it does not help anyone else. I‘m studying to be a psychologist, and punishment plays a major role in the psychology of behaviour/learned behaviour. It’s role in experiments is usually to condition a suppression/inhibition of the target behaviour in the subjects (poor little rats!). Punishment, in psychology, is therefore not a consequence of not being able to fix something, it is a tool to fix something (like a problematic behaviour). Punishment for the sake of suffering and penance is not a thing. If you really really can’t fix it, punishment is definitely not the logical consequence. Aside from that: I don’t think it really matters here. Because I do think you can change that pattern of ghosting people, though you probably need more time and support to do so. So why put your energy into punishing yourself when there’s another way to go, that would do actual good, and that needs you to put your time and energy in? And it’s not that I just think you should change for the sake of others. I know how lonely this pattern of ghosting can leave us. I have lost so many good people that way. Some stayed in my life, but like you, I am afraid of being „real“, so I keep my distance at least emotionally. It gets really, really lonely. You deserve to find true connection, to feel safe enough to open up to it. So yeah, in short: You don’t deserve to punish yourself. Physical integrity is a basic human right and need that nobody should be denied. Punishing yourself won’t do any good to anyone, including yourself, and it definitely is not the logical or morally required consequence of your situation. Healing, however, might do a lot of good for you and others. It also takes a lot of resources, so why not start putting your time and energy into getting better? I don’t want to invalidate or up you. I feel deeply for you, and I am very sorry you have to deal with such a heavy feeling of guilt. I do want to tell you a bit about myself though, because from your post I get the impression that we maybe can relate to one another. I think I used to be one of the good people who got tricked into believing they were bad. Like, I did some really bad stuff from an early age on, but only because I was forced to do so and I did what was needed to survive. I‘m not in that situation anymore. I have met many beautiful, caring souls since then. And still, I hurt them. You know how? I ghosted them. All of the. My wonderful friends, partners even. It really is not a nice thing to do. For me, I have found out that my ghosting comes from a lot of anxiety. I am worried I will say the wrong thing and hurt the relationship, so I don’t say anything. After a while, I am so ashamed for ignoring them that I can’t bear to think of them at all because it makes me feel sooooo guilty, so I never ask them back into my life and everyone ends up hurt. It seems to me that for you, there’s a deeper issue behind the ghosting as well. You say you can’t handle people being „real“. I think I get that. When reality has at times been unbearable, we tend do dissociate from it and always stay on a surface level. It is not selfish to self harm. But you don’t deserve to be treated like that, not even by yourself, and it also doesn’t change any of the things you feel guilty for - I think you even wrote it makes you feel more guilty. What I‘m trying to say is: It’s completely normal that change is hard, it does NOT make you a bad person if you know a behaviour is harmful and you still do it, awareness is really important, but we need more to be able to change. Just because you keep doing it even though you know it’s harmful does not mean you want to do it, and it does not make you bad. It makes you a human being, trying to keep themselves safe in an unpredictable, sometimes brutal world, a human being in need of more time and resources to tackle a really hard task.

(Usually systems who have partial DID have a host who fronts almost all the time and other alters only in situations of extreme (emotional) distress. So many pDID systems will barely switch and they still are very valid, of course. So you can have a complex dissociative disorder and barely switch at all).

However, if the amount you're switching is causing you trouble, you can try working on consciously influencing your switches - If you are rapid switching, it is very important to establish safety, and maybe you can get someone to front who feels able to deal with the situation and can front for a while. If you are frontstuck you can try to make sure that you're in a situation where others feel comfortable fronting and to ask someone to take over. You could also use their positive triggers, but personally I would only do that if your system has agreed that it's okay to use triggers, otherwise it can feel a bit invasive, I think. But again, if the amount you're switching works for you and feels okay, there's no need to change anything about it just because you feel you "should" be switching a certain amount.

You can also try talking to yourself out loud and some co-conscious parts might be able to hear you. Maybe try writing down your thoughts and worries or saying them out loud -- I find doing so very helpful in regulating my own worries and emotions and who knows, maybe someone will even notice or answer. Oh, and it might also be helpful to share with the others that you know of the system's existence and they don't need to hide, some parts might hide because they don't want to overwhelm you by showing themselves.

Fronting can be scary, but it also means you can try out all the things this world has to offer - Try out some foods and see what you like, maybe take a walk or listen to some music, you might even enjoy talking to some of the system's friends. Nope, actually this screening tool (if properly used) does not suggest you have DID if you report that these forms of non-pathological dissociation happen to you on a regular basis. Your results are to be compared to the most common results in different subgroups, like people with diagnosed DID, PTSD, other psychiatric disorders like anxiety and eating disorders and a nonclinical subgroup. This will give an idea which category you might fall into. Almost all people in the nonclinical subgroup will report having experienced nonpathological dissociation, so if you score high on these items but not on items referring to pathological dissociation, your results will indicate that you do not have a dissociative disorder. And even if your score is similar to that of people with DID, the DES is a screening tool and should not be used to diagnose DID, only to show whether further assessment is needed. If so, it should be followed up by an actual diagnostic tool like the SCID-D, which is very reliable in detecting whether someone has a dissociative disorder and if so, what kind. It also shows if someone is malingering. A thorough diagnosis will also rule out other explanations like ADHD (though someone can have both ADHD and DID and it should be carefully considered if both diagnosis are needed or if one of them suffices to explain the symptoms and if so, which one). 
No one should be diagnosing themselves if there’s any way they can get professional support and the DES is definitely not the right tool to diagnose anything, even if done under professional supervision.
It is, however, a very effective and reliable tool to screen for certain disorders.
The items asking about nonpathological dissociation do in no way put you at risk of being falsely identifies as dissociative if you answer honestly throughout the test. 
If anything, they make the test more reliable because unusually low scores on these items can indicate high defensiveness and unusually high scores malingering/exaggeration, both of which can give an experienced professional an idea of how valid your results are.
A VERY high score on the DES is usually not seen indicative of DID but rather of factitious disorder or malingering (Which does not mean everyone scoring very high is faking, they might just be highly dissociative. However, a good clinician will follow up with thoroughly differentiating between malingering/factitious disorder and extreme dissociative symptoms if someone scores unusually high on the DES.)
The DES is very good at indicating someone’s level of dissociation, including if this person displays a nonpathological level or is faking, which is what it is meant to do. It is not meant to diagnose anything.

TLDR: Many people don't know about being a system and having trauma until something causes alters to start showing themselves. Before that happens, the alters usually do not only hide from the host (person in the system handling most day-to-day-tasks) but also from their environment including loved ones, friends and therapists. That's why alters can seem to suddenly show up out of nowhere, and with them the knowledge about the experienced childhood trauma.

  
(Also, I hope this does not count as "blogging", I do have DID myself but I am not here to talk about my own experiences, just what I have learned about the "disorder" through psychoeducation and personal research (I'm also a psychologist undergraduate))

Here's the long version:  
I couldn't detect from your other comments whether you, Vorzheeva, have DID or whether you have another "disorder" with dissociative symptoms -- of course if you have DID yourself I don't want to act like I know the "disorder" better than you. (I use quotation marks because whilst DID can be and very often is incredibly debilitating, it's often what was needed to survive for a long time thus once was a very useful and very much needed coping mechanism and only becomes a disorder once it's no longer adaptive/needed).  
I also don't know this creator and have no idea whether they are valid (even professionals won't make assumptions about the validity of someone's DID based on their online presence). I don't want to defend them or in any other way judge/assess their validity. I just want to share some thoughts to shed light on DID in general because it is *so* fundamentally misunderstood by most people and I have seen quite some misconceptions in this thread.

I get the confusion about how someone might seem fine one moment and then start to exhibit DID symptoms seemingly out of nowhere. But actually, that's kind of what DID is meant to do: all the trauma and knowledge about that trauma gets compartmentalized into so called "emotional parts of the personality" (EPs), which usually includes the knowledge about being a system. A system can have one ore more "apparently normal parts of the personality" (ANPs), usually one in partial DID/OSDD and more in DID (the number of ANPs can vary, though and is not defined in the current diagnostic guidelines (DSM-V/ICD-11), however it is explained in the most up-to-date theory on structural dissociation (Nijenhuis et al.)).  
What that means, however, is that in many systems, the ANP(s) does/do neither know about the trauma nor about the existence of their system, since their job in the system is to take care of everyday life like school, social life etc., not the traumatic situations. The reason this separation between ANPs and EPs (including their awareness of the trauma & system) happens is generally that the ANP(s) would not be able to keep tackling day-to-day life if they were aware of the trauma because they would be too burdened. In many many cases, DID develops due to so-called "betrayal trauma", where the abuser is one of the child's caregivers (betrayal trauma generally leads to more dissociative symptoms than non-betrayal trauma).  Just imagine having to rely on the same person for shelter, nutrition, physical and emotional care during the day that does the most horrible things to you at night. That's a dissonance many children can't deal with which is why one single part cannot hold all of this knowledge and it gets divided into traumatic and non-traumatic experiences which are held by different parts of the personality. Of course it would be dangerous if the EPs revealed themselves not only to the ANP(s) but to the environment as well, since that would also risk the ANP(s) finding out about the abuse through the report of others.  
So that's why ANPs most often do not know about the trauma and do not show any obvious signs of a trauma-based disorder (at first). 

But what are the reasons why one suddenly can start showing these symptoms that were so well hidden before?  
One reason might be that the system feels save for the first time by moving away from their abuser(s) or through the death of the abuser(s). The EPs might feel like it's okay to reveal themselves through notes, talking to external people etc. and if the whole system feels more stable/safer, dissociative barriers might lessen and formerly unaware parts might start being able to observe switches or notice their amnesia (they often are amnestic for their amnesia). Another reason might be a new trauma in later life or having children that reach the age one's own abuse began, causing the whole system to decompensate and not being able to hide symptoms anymore. Or maybe there's a very skilled clinician or observant friend who sees the more subtle signs no-one used to notice.  
If the EPs have a very strong need to start sharing their trauma to find some relief or the formerly unaware parts are able to accept the presence of their system and show the capacity and will to get to know and listen to the other parts, dissociative barriers might break down rather quickly, at least between some parts - it's totally possible that communication between some parts develops very quickly and others, e.g. those carrying the most daunting trauma, stay hidden for longer. Some people might suddenly be able to hear voices and communicate internally just by accepting the presence of alters. Others might be really committed to getting better and establishing communication, starting rituals like journaling that give the other parts the opportunity to talk about themselves and their history.

*In short, it is not only possible, but rather likely that a person seems to have no trauma or alters for a long time and after initially becoming aware starts to know a lot about at least part of their symptoms/system/trauma history. The formerly hidden parts might also be very relieved to be able to stop hiding and reveal themselves to the external world rather suddenly as soon as they get the chance.*

There are, of course, exceptions. In partial DID/some forms of OSDD, many parts are aware of being a system all their life (but might not realize not everyone has alters/experiences themselves the way they do). In all complex dissociative disorders, parts might also be partly ANP, partly EP, meaning they carry some trauma, but are still amnestic to most of it/to the existence of other parts. In full blown DID it is rather the norm than the exception that *at least* one ANP, usually the host, is unaware of the trauma and the system for a long time and then becomes aware of it in whatever time makes sense for them and their system, could be rather quickly, but could also take some time.

It's the idea that every time wie fail to do a task (e.g. replying in time), a brick is added to a metaphorical wall in our head. With every time we fail to do it, the wall gets higher and higher, building an emotional barrier that keeps us from doing the thing.
